questions.q: Which API is the usual choice for extracting or loading very large tables on a schedule?
options: Bulk API
REST API
A browser bookmark
Report export by hand
questions.explain: The Bulk API processes large jobs asynchronously, which suits big scheduled extracts and loads.

questions.q: How does an integration typically authenticate to Salesforce without a person logging in?
options: By sharing an administrator's password in a script
By using OAuth 2.0 with a registered application and short-lived access tokens
By disabling authentication for API calls
By using the SOQL SELECT clause
questions.explain: OAuth 2.0 with a registered app (historically a connected app, increasingly an external client app) issues short-lived tokens.

questions.q: Which field lets a job fetch only records changed since its last successful run?
options: Name
RecordTypeId
SystemModstamp
OwnerId
questions.explain: SystemModstamp updates whenever a record changes, so it serves as a high-water mark for incremental pulls.

questions.q: Why should an integration run as a dedicated, least-privilege integration user?
options: Because API calls require an administrator profile
Because it removes all API limits
Because it lets the job ignore field-level security in reports
Because the user's permissions determine what the pipeline can see, and least privilege reduces risk
questions.explain: The running user's access decides which records and fields are returned, so it should be deliberate and minimal.

questions.q: What is the best approach to Salesforce API limits when designing an integration?
options: Look up your org's current limits, monitor usage, and design with incremental pulls and Bulk for volume
Ignore them until a job fails
Memorize one fixed number that applies to every org
Poll as often as possible for freshness
questions.explain: Limits vary by edition and license, so check your own and design to stay comfortably inside them.
